summary: Adds a simple extension to the Trivial File Transfer Protocol that lets client and server negotiate options before a file transfer starts. It was replaced by RFC 2347.

plainLanguage.summary: Before sending a file, the two sides can agree on how to do it, like picking box size.

questions: how to negotiate options in tftp
subtitle: Let TFTP clients and servers negotiate transfer options before sending data.

tldr.problem: TFTP is a simple lock-step file transfer protocol, but it lacks flexibility: there is no way for a client and server to agree on options like block size before starting the transfer.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC adds an option negotiation mechanism that lets options be appended to TFTP Read and Write requests, with a new OACK (Option Acknowledgment) packet type to confirm accepted options.
tldr.outcome: Servers and clients can now negotiate options like block size before the transfer, improving efficiency and compatibility. RFC 2347 later standardized this further.

today: RFC 1782 is a Proposed Standard that was superseded by RFC 2347, which standardized TFTP option extension further.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol) is a simple, lock-step protocol for transferring files over the network. However, it was designed with no way for clients and servers to agree on how to transfer a file before starting.

This RFC defines a backward-compatible extension to TFTP that allows option negotiation before the file transfer begins. The mechanism is kept simple by following TFTP's own request-respond-acknowledge sequence pattern. It was created to support the blocksize option (allowing larger transfers) defined in RFC 1783, and other options in RFC 1784.
sections.plainLanguage: TFTP is very simple, but sometimes a client and server want to agree on settings first, like how big chunks to send. This document adds a way to do that.

sections.title: Packet Formats
sections.content:
The extension adds options and their values to the end of TFTP Read Request (opcode 1) and Write Request (opcode 2) packets. Each option and value is NULL-terminated in ASCII, just like the original filename and mode fields. Multiple options can be appended in any order, and the total packet must not exceed 512 octets.

A new packet type, the Option Acknowledgment (OACK), is introduced with opcode 6. The OACK contains the same option/value pairs that the server accepts, in the same format. A new error code, 8, is defined to indicate that a transfer should be terminated due to option negotiation failure.
sections.plainLanguage: The client adds what it wants at the end of its request, like 'blksize' equals '1432'. The server sends back an OACK packet saying which options it agrees to.

sections.title: Negotiation Protocol
sections.content:
When a client appends options to a Read Request or Write Request, the server may respond with an OACK if it supports option negotiation and recognizes at least one option. The server includes only options it understands and accepts. Options that the server does not recognize are silently omitted from the OACK; they must not cause an error.

If the original request was a Read Request, the client confirms acceptance of the OACK by sending an ACK packet with block number 0. If the original request was a Write Request, the client confirms by starting the transfer with the first DATA packet using the negotiated values. If the client rejects the OACK, it sends an ERROR packet with error code 8. Once options are confirmed, both sides use only those options and values for the transfer.

If a server does not support option negotiation at all, it will ignore the appended options and respond with a normal DATA (for Read) or ACK (for Write) packet, starting the transfer as if no options were requested. This preserves backward compatibility.
sections.plainLanguage: The server says which options it will use. Then the client either agrees and sends back an ACK, or disagrees and sends an ERROR. If the server doesn't understand options at all, it just ignores them and sends back normal data.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
A Read Request asks for 'foofile' with a requested blocksize of 1432 octets. The server accepts with an OACK confirming blocksize 1432. The client acknowledges with ACK for block 0, then receives the file in 1432-octet blocks.

A Write Request asks to write 'barfile' with a requested blocksize of 2048 octets. The server accepts with an OACK confirming blocksize 2048. The client then sends the file in 2048-octet blocks, with the server acknowledging each block. In both cases, the negotiation precedes the actual data transfer, and once agreement is reached, the transfer uses the negotiated block size instead of the default 512 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: The client asks for a big block size like 1432 or 2048 bytes. The server says OK and sends an OACK back. Then they transfer the file using that block size instead of the tiny default.
